name: harvest dollies

attributes.attribute: folk figures made from the final sheaf taken at harvest
dressed in ribbon gowns and called maidens, figures of the ancient harvest goddess
kept near the hearth until the next year's doll replaced them
Scottish figure hung inside the house to protect the farm against fairy mischief

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Harvest dollies are Celtic folk figures. Until recent times the harvest celebration in Celtic lands carried rich meaning. On the Isle of Man people made straw images called mheillea, which means harvest, or baban ny mheillea, the doll of the harvest. They dressed the figures in ribbons to form gowns and called them maidens. Scholars see in them an ancient goddess of the abundant harvest. The figures stood about four inches tall and were often made from the final sheaf taken in. People kept the dolly near the hearth until the next year's doll replaced it. In Scotland a like "harvest maiden" protected the farm against fairy mischief when hung somewhere inside the house.

okr.objective: Document harvest dollies and their harvest goddess origins.
key_results: Record the Isle of Man names mheillea and baban ny mheillea.
Describe the straw maiden figure and its source in the harvest goddess.
Note the hearth keeping and the Scottish protective harvest maiden.
